# Preface {.unnumbered}

## Why this book?

Most biostatistics graduate curricula teach statistical theory
thoroughly. They teach practical data-analysis skill casually.
Students learn likelihood theory and the fine points of
hypothesis testing. Unfortunately, they arrive at their first
collaborative project unsure how to set up a project directory,
commit changes with `git`, parameterize a report, or write a
defensible statistical analysis plan.

We see this omission as structural rather than local to any one
program. A curriculum committee allocates credit hours to what
can be examined. The practice of analysis is hard to examine.
There is no closed-form answer to how a project should be
organized. Nor is there a problem set that separates a
compendium a stranger can rebuild from a directory of scripts
that produced the right numbers once. As a result, the skills a
biostatistician uses every working day are the ones the degree
least prepared them for. They are learned, if at all, by
apprenticeship and accident.

This book aims to close that gap. We teach the practical skills
needed to do reproducible biostatistical work in 2026: the
tools, the workflows, and the professional norms. We assume
throughout that the reader is also studying a theory-heavy
statistical computing course alongside this one, and we treat
modeling as that course's territory rather than our own.

## Why now

A book of this kind would have been useful in 2015. We consider
it necessary in 2026. Three developments have changed what a
competent biostatistician is expected to do.

**Reproducibility stopped being a virtue and became a
requirement.** For two decades the case for reproducible
analysis was made on scientific grounds
[@peng2011reproducible; @goodman2016what]. It was widely read as
good advice. It was not read as an obligation. That changed when
funders made reproducibility a formal requirement. The 2022
memorandum from the White House Office of Science and Technology
Policy [@usshi2022ostp] directs every federal research funder to
require immediate public access to publications and to the data
underlying them. Agencies were to implement the policy by the
end of 2025. Since January 2023, every NIH application has carried a
Data Management and Sharing Plan that becomes a term of the
award. The FDA has required CDISC-conformant submissions since
2016. A graduate entering the field now will be asked, in their
first year, to name a repository, produce a persistent
identifier, and state how the computational environment will be
preserved. A theory sequence does not prepare students to
answer these questions. Yet the statistician is the team member
most likely to be asked them. @sec-federal covers these policies directly.
The rest of the book is, in effect, the technical answer to it.

**Large language models shifted the bottleneck from writing code
to auditing it.** By 2026 a competent model produces working R
for most of the exercises in this book. It also produces a
substantial share of the analysis code a junior statistician is
asked to write. That changes what expertise consists of. The parts of the work a model does well are the
mechanical parts this book teaches quickly. The parts it does
badly are the judgments this book spends most of its pages on. A
model will not tell you that your discussion section overstates
what your design supports. It will not tell you that the join
you just wrote inflated the denominator. Nor will it tell you
that the study was not powered for the subgroup you are about to
report. It will, however, write the join. By 2026 much of that
code is written by an agent. An agent is a tool that reads the
codebase, edits several files, and runs the result. It does more
than a chat window that returns a single answer to copy. An
agent lets a mistake spread faster and further. The analyst is
still responsible for catching it. If we ignored these tools,
students would discover their failure modes on real projects.
Teaching the tools without teaching verification would be worse.
@sec-ai-coding addresses the question directly. Every chapter
also closes with prompts paired with an explicit verification
step.

**The tooling finally settled.** Until recently, the tools this
book teaches changed from year to year. Quarto matured and took
over much of the role of R Markdown. The `renv` package
[@ushey2026renv] replaced `packrat` and became the default for
project-level dependency pinning. The `rocker` images
[@boettiger2017rocker] made containerized R routine. The
`targets` package [@landau2021targets] gave R a dependency-aware
build tool that fits how analysts actually work. A book written
in 2018 would have taught tools that are now deprecated. The
tools described here are stable enough to be worth learning.
They are also recent enough that most working biostatisticians
were never taught them.

## What the peer curricula do and do not cover

Several chapters of this book are motivated by a survey of the
published graduate curricula of peer United States
biostatistics programs. We list the sources in @sec-peer-survey
so that the reader can check the claim.

The published curricula concentrate, reasonably, on statistical
computing in the algorithmic sense: optimization, simulation
design, the bootstrap, and Bayesian computation. The gaps tend
to fall in the practical work between a method and a result a
reader can trust. The command line, SQL
and database extraction, principled missing-data practice,
dependency-aware pipelines, continuous integration, and
de-identification each appear in a minority of published
curricula. Each is something a biostatistician will be asked to
do within months of starting work. When a chapter exists
because of such a gap, it says so at the start and cites the
evidence.

Two topics deserve particular mention. Alumni report directly
that their absence has a cost. The first is CDISC
(@sec-cdisc). Graduates entering pharmaceutical and
contract-research positions encounter SDTM and ADaM in their
first week and find that no course prepared them. The second is
SAS (@sec-sas), which remains the screening filter for a large
share of United States industry positions, regardless of what
one thinks of the language. Neither chapter argues that these
standards are good. Both argue that a graduate who cannot read
them is shut out of work they are otherwise qualified for.

## Craft is not separable from correctness

Analysis is error-prone. Many of its errors are caught by
infrastructure and missed by vigilance. That is why the
infrastructure in this book exists. Consider three failures. A
join silently multiplies rows. A package update changes a
function's behavior between the analysis and the revision. A
figure is built from an intermediate file that was not rebuilt
after the cleaning script changed. None of these is visible when
it happens, and being careful does not catch them. Each is
caught by an assertion, a lockfile, or a dependency graph.
Reproducible infrastructure is a courtesy to future readers. Its
more immediate benefit is practical. The work of a statistician
consists of ten or fifteen simultaneous projects
[@slade2023team]. The infrastructure keeps each of them from
deteriorating unnoticed.

These tools also have a limit. A perfectly reproducible, fully
compliant, numerically correct analysis can still mislead every
reader it reaches. No automated check catches that kind of
failure. @sec-ethics addresses this problem. Its argument is
that none of the infrastructure in this book determines whether
an analysis misleads. We place the chapter late because the
argument makes the most sense after the reader has built that
infrastructure.

## What is different here

- **Reproducibility is the organizing principle.** Each chapter
  is framed around producing analyses that a collaborator can
  rerun and extend.
- **Judgment is taught directly.** Every chapter contains a
  section on what the tool cannot decide for you. These
  decisions separate defensible practice from competent tool
  use. Neither a package nor a model makes them for you.
- **AI-assisted workflows are covered.** Students in 2026 will
  use large language models in their daily work, often through
  coding agents that read and edit a project directly. One
  chapter covers using these tools responsibly in R work. Every
  chapter ends with prompts designed to expose their limits,
  each paired with a verification step.
- **Real case studies.** Two full analyses (Palmer Penguins and
  ADNI MCI prediction) are carried end-to-end, from project
  scaffolding to final report.
- **Federal context.** Biostatisticians working on federally
  funded research must meet NIH/NSF reproducibility
  requirements. A dedicated chapter covers what those
  requirements are and how to satisfy them.
- **The collaborative reality.** The biostatistician's work is
  done on teams, across several projects at once, with
  colleagues who cannot read the code. @sec-team-science treats
  working this way as a skill that can be learned.

## Prerequisites

Readers should have:

- An undergraduate statistics background.
- Basic R familiarity (subsetting, the pipe, writing functions).
  Readers who lack this should first work through the early
  chapters of the companion book or *R for Data Science*
  [@wickham2023r4ds].
- Access to R 4.4+, RStudio (optional), and Git.

No prior Docker, `renv`, or Quarto experience is assumed.

## Conventions

See the [Conventions](conventions.qmd) page for the visual
cues used throughout the book.

## Assigning parts of this book

Instructors are welcome to assign individual chapters rather
than the whole book. The book is designed to allow this. Every
chapter opens with a card listing what it assumes, what the
reader will be able to do, and an outline. A short quiz follows
for readers who may be able to skip the chapter. Because the
book is free, assigning a few chapters costs students nothing.

However, the chapters do depend on one another, as
@fig-book-map in @sec-intro shows. Parts I through III give the
reader the reasons, the toolkit, and data in hand. Part IV makes
that work reproducible. Parts V and VI apply it to analysis
plans, testing, and industry standards. A chapter from Part V or
VI can be assigned on its own to a reader who already has a
working environment. A reader without one will need to go back
several parts. The case studies in Part VII and the
capstone in Part VIII assume everything above them.

## Course length and the one-quarter core

The book is written for a two-quarter sequence at about two
chapters a week. The first quarter covers why reproducibility
matters, the working toolkit, and getting data in and into
shape. The toolkit includes `renv`, Docker, and the research
compendium, so a project rebuilds on another machine from the
first weeks. The second quarter covers Quarto documents and
pipelines, analysis practice, industry standards, and the case
studies, and ends in a capstone. A semester course can cover most of the book at the
same pace.

A one-quarter course should use the core path below: twenty
chapters, two a week for ten weeks. It includes the skills a new
analyst needs in the first week on the job, and the habits the
rest of the book builds on. The remaining chapters are written
to be picked up later, alone or in a second course.

| Week | Core chapters |
|---|---|
| 1 | [Why Reproducible Research](#sec-why); [De-identification and Data Ethics](#sec-deident) |
| 2 | [Setting Up Your Workstation](#sec-workstation); [Git and GitHub for Solo Developers](#sec-git-solo) |
| 3 | [Git for Teams](#sec-git-teams); [renv for Package Management](#sec-renv) |
| 4 | [Docker for Reproducibility](#sec-docker); [Assembling the Compendium](#sec-zzcollab) |
| 5 | [AI-Assisted Coding](#sec-ai-coding); [Getting Data In](#sec-acquisition) |
| 6 | [Data Wrangling Essentials](#sec-wrangling); [Joining and Reshaping](#sec-joins) |
| 7 | [Plotting with ggplot2 and purrr](#sec-graphics); [Missing Data](#sec-missing) |
| 8 | [Reproducible Reports with Quarto](#sec-quarto); [Statistical Analysis Plans](#sec-analysis-plan) |
| 9 | [Testing and Continuous Integration](#sec-testing); [Ethics Beyond Compliance](#sec-ethics) |
| 10 | [Case Study: Palmer Penguins](#sec-penguins); [Communicating a Finished Analysis](#sec-communicating) |

Outside the core, and suited to the second quarter or to
independent reading: @sec-team-science, @sec-apis, @sec-types,
@sec-deident-practice, @sec-targets, @sec-cloud, @sec-cdisc,
@sec-sas, @sec-adni, @sec-federal, and the capstone in
@sec-synthesis. Two chapters are optional for everyone:
@sec-shell, for readers new to the terminal, and
@sec-databases, for readers whose data live in a database. Students heading
to the pharmaceutical industry should add @sec-cdisc and
@sec-sas to the core.
